meaning: "Heaven" — the sky-realm of the orisha, the divine order above the world

pronunciation.note: Ọrun is Yoruba for 'heaven': the precomposed dot-below Ọ is the domain-maximal form — the full tone marks (Ọ̀run, low-high) cannot be registered as a domain, so the temple preserves the tone in text while the address bar carries what the DNS allows. The dot-below is the open-mid vowel — the open aw of law — distinct from the close o; the tone is low-high, rising from the grave to the acute.

kin.label: Yoruba
kin.form: Ọ̀run — the fully tone-marked form: grave on the ọ, acute on the ú; tone is grammatical in Yoruba (Abraham, Dictionary of Modern Yoruba, s.v. ọrun)

kin.label: Owner of heaven
kin.form: Olóòrun — 'owner of heaven', the supreme being's title, built from the same word (Idowu, Olódùmarè)

kin.form: Ọrun — the precomposed dot-below form carried in the domain; it preserves the open vowel the ASCII 'orun' flattens

domains.title: The Heaven Above the Heavens
domains.subtitle: Sky, Destiny, and the Realm of Olódùmarè
domains.lead: Ọrun is the Yoruba name of heaven itself: the sky-realm where Olódùmarè and the orisha dwell, from which every soul descends to earth (ayé) — and to which every destiny (orí) is assigned before birth. It is not a god but the address of the gods.

cards.name: Ọrun and Ayé
cards.desc: Heaven and earth: the two halves of reality, with the soul commuting between them.

cards.name: Orí
cards.desc: The inner head — the personal destiny each soul chooses (or receives) in Ọrun before birth.

cards.name: Olódùmarè
cards.desc: The Owner of Heaven — the supreme being whose realm Ọrun is.

cards.name: The Descent
cards.desc: Every birth is an emigration from heaven; every death, the return journey.

symbols.name: The white cloth
symbols.meaning: Heaven's color — purity and the unblemished sky

symbols.name: The palm nuts
symbols.meaning: Ifá's instruments — heaven's messages read on earth

symbols.name: The head
symbols.meaning: Orí, the chosen destiny — heaven carried inside the skull

symbols.name: The golden chain
symbols.meaning: The road from Ọrun down which the first orisha descended to found Ilé-Ifẹ̀ — and by which every soul since has commuted between heaven and earth

mythology.lead: Ọrun's myths are the architecture of Yoruba cosmology: how heaven was connected to earth, how every soul is commissioned before birth, and how the traffic between the two realms has never once stopped.

myths.title: The Chain to Earth
myths.text: In the beginning there was only sky. Below Ọrun lay the primeval waters, and on the water floated nothing but the command of Olódùmarè. The creation account recorded across Yorubaland — set down by the Rev. Samuel Johnson in the early twentieth century and analyzed by Bolaji Idowu — tells how Olódùmarè sent the orisha down a golden chain from heaven with a hen, a chameleon, and a handful of sand. Where the sand fell and the hen scratched, a mound rose from the flood: Ilé-Ifẹ̀, 'the house that spreads', the navel of the earth. The chain did not come back up; it anchored heaven to the new ground, and orisha, ancestors, and newborn souls have traveled it in both directions ever since. The myth means that Yoruba cosmology is a story of migration. Every birth repeats the first descent, and the road between Ọrun and ayé has never once been closed.

myths.title: The Choosing of Orí
myths.text: Before a child is born, the Ifá corpus teaches, its soul kneels in Ọrun at the workshop of Ajala, the celestial potter, to choose its orí — the inner head that is its personal destiny. The odu narratives (see Abimbola, Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus, and Bascom, Ifá Divination) tell of souls who chose carelessly, who bargained, or who arrived too late and had to take whatever heads remained. The choice is then sealed and the memory wiped: the child is born carrying an unread contract, and life is the slow reading of it. This is why Yoruba religion lavishes its attention on the head itself — offerings are made to the orí, the physical crown of the body, the one shrine every person carries everywhere. The myth means that destiny is chosen, not imposed — but chosen by a self you no longer remember being.

myths.title: Souls on the Road
myths.text: The Yoruba cosmos runs on commuting. Orisha descend to mount their priests in trance; ancestors return as Egúngún masquerades; the dead are reborn, and the abíkú — 'born to die' — are the children who keep commuting, slipping back to Ọrun young and being sent down again until their earthly parents find a charm to bind them to stay. The Ifá verses speak of these journeys as ordinary travel — dangerous, expensive, but routine — along the same chain-road the first orisha descended (Abimbola; Bascom; Drewal). The dead do not leave the world; they change direction. The myth means that Ọrun is not a distant heaven but an adjacent one — the next town, not the next world — and the border is crossed so often that every lineage keeps stories of the crossing.

myths.title: The Egúngún Come Back
myths.text: The most dramatic proof that the dead commute is the Egúngún: the masked, robed masqueraders who appear at the great festivals and are understood — not metaphorically but literally — as ancestors returned from Ọrun for a visit. The cloth-wrapped figure may never be touched or unmasked, for the cloth is both its embassy and its disguise; its voice is disguised, its blessing is sought by the whole lineage, and its displeasure is feared more than any chief's (Drewal, Pemberton and Abiodun, Yoruba: Nine Centuries of African Art and Thought, 1989). The Egúngún societies keep the costumes as lineage treasures handed down the generations, and the appearance of the ancestors is the high point of the ritual year. The institution means that heaven maintains a postal service: the dead can still speak, still bless, still scold — they simply cannot stay, and the message always comes wrapped in cloth.

lore.syncretism: The Ọrun-ayé structure traveled with the diaspora: Candomblé's Oxalá-realm, Santería's heaven of Olófin, and Haiti's lwa-cosmology all keep the two-world map. Christian heaven merged with Ọrun in the New World without ever absorbing it: the Yoruba sky remains a realm of traffic and traffic-officers (the orisha), not of distant thrones — heaven as the next city over, not the next world.
lore.culturalLegacy: The word lives in a thousand names: Ọrunmila (heaven-knows-salvation), Ọlọrun (owner-of-heaven), Ọrúnmìlà, Ọba-Ọrun. Ifá divination — UNESCO-listed — is its daily news service, and the Egúngún festivals keep the ancestors' visits on the calendar. Every Yoruba funeral says the same thing in ten thousand voices: 'the journey to Ọrun is well-traveled' — heaven as home, not as hope.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Ọrun is the heaven you came from, not the one you hope to reach. Every soul descends with an orí already chosen and the memory of the choice erased: you signed the contract, but the signature is in a language you no longer speak. Yoruba religion is therefore not a quest for heaven but a negotiation with the heaven already inside — the head you chose is the life you are living.

And the traffic never stops. The babaláwo casts the palm-nuts at dawn, the Egúngún walk at noon, a child is named for heaven by evening. Ọrun is the least distant heaven ever conceived — next door, upstairs, on the line. The question is never whether it answers; it is whether we are still calling.

lore.archaeology: Ilé-Ifẹ̀, the city founded on the scattered earth, keeps the creation-site shrines: the Oke Itase hill and the palace of the Ọọni, whose crown descends from heaven's own. The bronze and terracotta heads of Ifẹ̀ (12th–15th c.), among Africa's supreme artworks, are the faces of heaven's first citizens. The Ifá corpus — the great oral archive — is preserved by the babaláwo lineages of Yorubaland and the diaspora.
